name: Zinc oxide mineral sunscreen

lead: Zinc oxide sunscreens give broad UVA and UVB protection using a mineral filter, and people use them for slower photoaging and even skin tone, often on sensitive or acne-prone skin and for daily facial use.

Zinc oxide is the broadest-spectrum UV filter approved by the FDA for sunscreen and is photostable. With titanium dioxide, it was one of two filters the FDA categorized as GRASE as of 2021. Nanoscale versions exist to reduce white cast, and studies of nanoparticle zinc oxide on human skin found very low penetration.

paras: People apply it as a lotion, cream or stick over the face and body, daily and before outdoor time, and reapply after sweating or swimming. Tinted or nano formulations are chosen to reduce the visible white film.
The usual complaint is white cast on the skin, especially on deeper skin tones. Laboratory work has examined zinc release under UV and combinations with organic filters.

chain: Mineral filter blocks UVA and UVB
angle.text: Zinc oxide sunscreens are used by people who want broad-spectrum, photostable protection, often for sensitive or acne-prone skin and daily facial use. It blocks UVA and UVB, slowing photoaging and keeping tone even; the white cast is its main drawback.

lead: Zinc oxide mineral sunscreen uses zinc oxide, an inorganic (mineral) compound, as its active ultraviolet filter. Zinc oxide protects against both UVA and UVB light and, with titanium dioxide, is one of the two mineral filters used in sunscreens.[1]

Wikipedia describes it as the broadest-spectrum UVA and UVB absorber approved by the US FDA for sunscreen and as photostable.[2] As of 2021 zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were the only sunscreen filters the FDA categorized as generally recognized as safe and effective (GRASE).[1]

Much published research concerns nanoparticulate zinc oxide, which is used to avoid the white appearance of conventional mineral products. Studies using skin-penetration assays and in vivo microscopy have examined whether the particles pass through human skin.[3][4]

For appearance, daily sunscreen is the step people use to limit sun-related skin ageing and uneven tone, and zinc oxide is the filter often chosen for it. A 2025 Delphi consensus of cosmetic dermatologists, with 62 dermatologists at 43 centres, listed mineral sunscreen among the topical ingredients they recommend for fine lines and wrinkles and for redness [5].

paras: Wikipedia states that mineral filters work mainly by absorbing UV light, with some reflection and scattering.[1] Early-2000s research cited there suggested zinc oxide performed better than titanium dioxide at 340 to 380 nm in the UVA range.[1]

Mineral sunscreens can leave a visible white cast, which the sunscreen article says some consumers dislike and which may lead some to apply them more thinly.[1] Nanoscale zinc oxide does not scatter visible light as strongly, so products look less white.[2] A patent family describes powder blends of zinc oxide and titanium dioxide with defined size distributions for sunscreens.
In the US, labels do not need to disclose whether mineral ingredients are nanoparticles, while the EU requires disclosure.[1]

A 2007 in vitro study using Franz diffusion cells and electron microscopy on human epidermis found that less than 0.03 percent of the applied zinc from a micronized zinc oxide formulation penetrated.[3] A 2020 review of ten years of in vivo multiphoton microscopy work on human skin concluded that it had been used to assess whether nanoparticulate zinc oxide penetrates, in a period when a precautionary approach to nanoparticles in consumer products was being argued.[4]

A 2010 laboratory study reported that UVB irradiation could release zinc ions from commercial zinc oxide sunscreen and examined the effect of zinc accumulation on cultured human keratinocytes.[6] Wikipedia notes that some zinc is slightly absorbed into skin, and describes zinc oxide as non-toxic in sunscreen use, with fumes from industrial heating a separate hazard.[2] Wikipedia also mentions a case in which combinations of zinc oxide and small-molecule organic absorbers showed photodegradation and toxicity in zebrafish embryos.[2]

The US FDA's consumer guidance lists zinc oxide and titanium dioxide among the active ingredients in sunscreens and explains that broad-spectrum products protect against both UVA and UVB, that SPF indicates mainly UVB (sunburn) protection, and that products that are not broad spectrum or have an SPF below 15 must carry a skin cancer and skin aging warning [7].

Because the white cast is the main aesthetic complaint, manufacturers have developed tinted and sheer mineral products. A 12-week open-label study of a sheer 100 percent mineral sunscreen moisturizer with SPF 50 enrolled 39 women aged 35 to 60 with moderate to severe facial photodamage across all Fitzpatrick skin types, measured with grading, photography, ultrasound imaging and corneometer readings at weeks 4, 8 and 12, and reported statistically significant progressive improvements, with mean improvements of about 23 to 27 percent in the measures reported at week 12 [8].

A 2026 study examined visible-light protection in tinted inorganic sunscreens, noting that visible light and long-wavelength UVA1 have been reported to cause erythema in light skin and to worsen pigmentary conditions such as melasma in darker skin [9].

A 2007 study compared an organic filter and a mineral filter (titanium dioxide) in a broad-spectrum formulation using tape stripping in vivo and compartmental in vitro methods, to see whether they penetrate beyond the surface layers of the stratum corneum [10]. Together with the zinc oxide studies cited above, such work addresses the question of whether mineral particles reach living tissue.

No clinical trials of zinc oxide sunscreen on appearance outcomes were found. Human skin-penetration studies exist: an in vitro study on excised human epidermis and in vivo multiphoton microscopy studies.[3][4]

lore.intro: Mineral sunscreen is discussed in grooming and skin-care forums as a gentler or more 'natural' alternative to chemical filters, with the white cast the recurring complaint.[11]
